text: Checking what's actually cached for this procedure, creation_time shows exactly when this plan was compiled. Cross-checking against the clinic's own change log shows that's the same morning the part-time provider was the very first person whose schedule got pulled up, right after an overnight statistics update forced a recompile.

Don't just infer it, prove it. Force a fresh recompile with sp_recompile, then run the typical provider first, so the new plan compiles for them. Run the part-time provider second. That's a controlled experiment: change one thing, which provider compiles the plan first, and the fast and slow pattern flips completely. The procedure's text never changed at any point.

SQL Server compiles one plan per procedure and caches it, optimized for the specific parameter value passed in on that first call. For the part-time provider with very few appointments, the optimizer chose a seek-based plan, correct for a handful of rows. Every later call reuses that same cached plan regardless of which provider is actually passed in next.

This is parameter sniffing: the plan is correct for the parameter it was sniffed with, and wrong for everyone else. For a typical provider with hundreds of appointments, that same seek-based plan is a poor fit, but it's still the plan that runs, because SQL Server doesn't automatically recompile just because a different value came in.

Nothing about the stored procedure's T-SQL is wrong. The bug is in which value happened to compile the cached plan, which depends on something as arbitrary as whose schedule got pulled up first after a recompile — exactly why no code change didn't rule this out. The plan changed; the code never did.
